interest: Japan's constitution and the South Seas Mandate, the Kellogg-Briand Pact and the London Naval Treaty.
overview: State Department decimal file 894.011 (covering 1923 to 1940) documents U.S. diplomatic monitoring of the Meiji Constitution of Japan (1889) and its domestic and international legal implications. The file opens with a 1923 despatch reporting debates in the House of Peers over whether the Japanese Constitution applied to the South Seas Mandate, followed by a 1925 despatch transmitting a complete official English translation of the 76-article constitution. Subsequent cross-reference sheets from 1929 and 1930 highlight critical controversies involving constitutional interpretation, including Japanese objections to the phrase 'in the names of their respective peoples' in the Kellogg-Briand Anti-War Pact and the profound constitutional crisis over the London Naval Treaty regarding the Emperor's supreme command over the military. The file is rounded out by 1932 correspondence answering an American citizen's request for copies of the constitution and internal State Department record charge slips from 1936 and 1940.

subfiles.about: Presents the full text in English translation of the 1889 Constitution of the Empire of Japan (Meiji Constitution).
subfiles.summary: This enclosure provides a complete English translation of the Meiji Constitution across seven chapters and 76 articles. It delineates the sacred and inviolable sovereignty of the Emperor, imperial prerogatives over the military and lawmaking, and the rights and duties of Japanese subjects. It also specifies the composition and procedures of the Imperial Diet (House of Peers and House of Representatives), the role of Ministers of State and the Privy Council, the judicature, financial management, and procedures for constitutional amendment.
subfiles.title: English Translation of the Constitution of the Empire of Japan (Meiji Constitution)
